\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We introduced ordinal generation depth estimation as a task for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive LLM generation.
In a controlled study of eight base-model generators from five families (0.6B--8B parameters), we documented differential depth response: central-tendency features drift monotonically while upper-tail features remain near-stationary, consistent with recursive generation inducing a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation.
A 7-feature ensemble achieves binary F1\,=\,0.694 for leak-free depth discrimination (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+), and cross-model chains (five-generator subset) confirm signal persistence under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764).
Depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality, indicating that depth composition per se does not determine training utility.

These results establish depth fingerprinting as a tool for understanding recursive generation phenomena in base models.
Extending to instruction-tuned models (where depth signal degrades substantially) and frontier-scale generators (70B+) are priorities for future work.
All code, data, and trained models will be released upon publication to facilitate reproducibility.

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Recursive application of language models, where each generation step conditions on prior LLM output, produces text with progressively altered distributional properties.
We study this phenomenon under controlled conditions, restricting to base (pretrained) models to isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth rather than a binary real-vs-synthetic label, and characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency features drift monotonically with depth while upper-tail shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution with partial shape preservation.
A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this complementarity achieves F1\,=\,0.764 on heterogeneous cross-model chains (a different generator at each depth) and generalizes to entirely unseen generators under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.694), significantly outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
We additionally report that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself (how distributional features evolve across generation depths) remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using eight base (pretrained) models from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable for depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation; under this account, the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input content, while variance shows moderate drift.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves 3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains).
However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

We additionally report a negative finding: despite the effectiveness of quality-based data curation for pretraining \cite{fineweb,dolma}, depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
        \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across eight base-model generators spanning five model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains and binary F1\,=\,0.694 under strict unseen-generator evaluation, with a single lightweight reference model, significantly outperforming individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.

We evaluate whether depth signal generalizes beyond Wikipedia by constructing generation chains from three additional domains: News articles, Academic abstracts, and Code documentation.
For each domain, we sample 200 seed texts and generate chains of depth 3 using three generators (Pythia-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, Mistral-7B).
The same 7-feature ensemble and LOGO protocol are applied.

\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-domain depth classification under LOGO evaluation (binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Three generators $\times$ 200 seeds per domain. Bootstrap 95\% CIs ($n$\,=\,1000).}
\label{tab:domain}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Domain} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{3-class F1} \\
\midrule
Code           & 0.754 & [0.737, 0.770] & 0.634 \\
News           & 0.746 & [0.726, 0.764] & 0.652 \\
Academic       & 0.739 & [0.720, 0.757] & 0.622 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All three non-Wikipedia domains achieve binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, demonstrating that depth signal is not an artifact of Wikipedia text properties.

\paragraph{Temperature caveat.}
Cross-domain generation used $t{=}1.0$, top-$p{=}1.0$ (vs.\ the main experiment's $t{=}0.7$, top-$p{=}0.9$).
The sampling sensitivity analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows that $t{=}1.0$ reduces classification F1 by approximately 6\,pp relative to $t{=}0.7$.
The reported cross-domain F1 values therefore represent a conservative lower bound; domain-matched evaluation at $t{=}0.7$ would likely yield higher scores.
This temperature confound prevents direct comparison with the main Wikipedia results, but the absolute performance (F1 $>$ 0.73 under both domain shift and aggressive decoding) provides strong evidence that depth fingerprinting is domain-general.

\paragraph{3-class inversion as DDR evidence.}
In the cross-domain setting, 3-class F1 (0.62--0.65) falls below binary F1 (0.74--0.75), reversing the pattern observed in the main experiment (3-class 0.762 $>$ binary 0.694).

The binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) is unaffected because both classes are generated under identical domain and decoding conditions; recursive drift is a relative change that does not depend on absolute calibration.
This pattern provides additional evidence that DDR captures generation-process invariants rather than domain-specific text properties: depth signal remains robust even when the human-vs-machine boundary becomes less distinct.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO); a moderate performance gap relative to the main experiment is partially attributable to the more aggressive decoding parameters ($t{=}1.0$) used for cross-domain generation.

\section*{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All eight generators are base (pretrained) models.
This is a deliberate design choice: base models isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects, enabling controlled study of recursive distributional drift.
However, web text is predominantly produced by instruction-tuned and RLHF-aligned models.
Preliminary instruct experiments confirm that depth signal degrades substantially under instruction tuning: OLMo-2-1B-Instruct drops to LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 (vs.\ 0.764 base) and Qwen3-0.6B with chat template to 0.667 (vs.\ 0.816 under a 7-generator split).
Length-matched analysis yields near-zero correlations ($|\rho| < 0.02$) and binary classification near chance (F1\,$\approx$\,0.5) for Qwen models, leaving interpretation ambiguous.
Extending depth fingerprinting to instruct models requires addressing these confounds (length regulation, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that instruction tuning introduces.

Our experiments include generators up to 8.2B parameters (Qwen3-8B).
Depth signal persists at this scale (Qwen3-8B 3-class F1\,=\,0.714), but cross-scale transfer incurs a moderate gap vs.\ $\leq$2.8B generators (F1\,=\,0.77--0.81).
Frontier models (70B+) remain untested; their higher fluency may further compress feature margins.

Differential depth response strength is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains show strongest drift (within-type F1\,=\,0.781) compared to elaboration (0.730), rewriting (0.737), and paraphrastic chains (binary F1\,=\,0.671 vs.\ 0.749 for continuation).
DDR is most reliably detected in continuation-style generation; near-paraphrastic settings approach the method's detection floor.
Cross-prompt-type transfer (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753) confirms shared signal, yet additional prompt types (e.g., summarization, instruction following) and cross-generator $\times$ cross-prompt interactions remain untested.

Our primary evaluation uses single-generator chains; cross-model chains (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}) confirm depth signal under generator heterogeneity (3-class F1\,=\,0.809, binary F1\,=\,0.764), though the eight generators represent a controlled laboratory setting rather than the full diversity of real-world contamination.
Simulated human editing (\S\ref{sec:discussion}) suggests graceful degradation, but the gap between simulated token replacement and real-world post-processing remains untested.

The reference model is fixed to Pythia-410M throughout, although cross-family reference experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm the phenomenon is not reference-specific (spread 0.013 across three references).
All seed texts in the main evaluation are English Wikipedia excerpts.
Cross-domain evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}) shows that depth signal persists across News, Academic, and Code domains (binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under LOGO at $t{=}1.0$), though a domain $\times$ temperature interaction exists: certain domain/generator combinations at lower temperature approach chance level (e.g., Academic domain binary F1\,=\,0.628 at $t{=}0.7$), suggesting that reference model calibration is critical for cross-domain deployment.
Generalization to other languages remains untested.

Our default analysis uses fixed decoding parameters (temperature 0.7, nucleus $p{=}0.9$). A sampling ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}) shows robustness to moderate variation ($t \in [0.5, 0.7]$, ${\leq}0.3$\,pp) but substantial degradation at $t{=}1.0$ ($-6$\,pp), indicating that depth fingerprinting assumes standard decoding regimes.

We use 3-class granularity (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+). A 5-class evaluation (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}) yields LOGO F1\,$\approx$\,0.50, with depths 2--4 mutually indistinguishable, validating the 3-class design as the practical resolution limit.

We evaluate whether depth signal generalizes beyond Wikipedia by constructing generation chains from three additional domains: News articles, Academic abstracts, and Code documentation.
For each domain, we sample 200 seed texts and generate chains of depth 3 using three generators (Pythia-1B, Qwen3-1.7B, Mistral-7B).
The same 7-feature ensemble and LOGO protocol are applied.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-domain depth classification under LOGO evaluation (binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+). Three generators $\times$ 200 seeds per domain. Bootstrap 95\% CIs ($n$\,=\,1000).}
\label{tab:domain}
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Domain} & \textbf{Binary F1} & \textbf{95\% CI} & \textbf{3-class F1} \\
\midrule
Code           & 0.754 & [0.737, 0.770] & 0.634 \\
News           & 0.746 & [0.726, 0.764] & 0.652 \\
Academic       & 0.739 & [0.720, 0.757] & 0.622 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

All three non-Wikipedia domains achieve binary F1 $>$ 0.73 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, demonstrating that depth signal is not an artifact of Wikipedia text properties.

\paragraph{Domain $\times$ temperature interaction.}
Cross-domain generation used $t{=}1.0$, top-$p{=}1.0$ (vs.\ the main experiment's $t{=}0.7$, top-$p{=}0.9$).
Supplementary evaluation at $t{=}0.7$ reveals a domain $\times$ temperature interaction: the main Wikipedia experiment favors lower temperature ($t{=}0.7$ yields +6\,pp over $t{=}1.0$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), while cross-domain evaluation favors higher temperature ($t{=}1.0$ yields +3 to +11\,pp over $t{=}0.7$; News 0.746 vs.\ 0.712, Academic 0.739 vs.\ 0.628, Code 0.754 vs.\ 0.687).
This asymmetry likely reflects reference-model calibration: Pythia-410M, trained predominantly on web text, detects subtle per-step drift in Wikipedia but requires larger distributional divergence (produced by higher temperature) to detect depth signal in out-of-distribution domains.
This finding suggests that reference model selection is a key factor for cross-domain deployment of depth fingerprinting.

\paragraph{3-class inversion as DDR evidence.}
In the cross-domain setting, 3-class F1 (0.62--0.65) falls below binary F1 (0.74--0.75), reversing the pattern observed in the main experiment (3-class 0.762 $>$ binary 0.694).
This inversion reflects degraded gen-0 vs.\ gen-1 separation: the Pythia-410M reference model is calibrated to Wikipedia text, so its baseline entropy estimates are less discriminative for out-of-domain human text, compressing the feature distance between gen-0 and gen-1.
The binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) is unaffected because both classes are generated under identical domain and decoding conditions; recursive drift is a relative change that does not depend on absolute calibration.
This pattern provides additional evidence that DDR captures generation-process invariants rather than domain-specific text properties: depth signal remains robust even when the human-vs-machine boundary becomes less distinct.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-crawled corpora increasingly contain LLM-generated text (estimates suggest that 7--17\% of recent scientific papers and peer reviews contain substantial LLM-modified content \cite{mapping_llm_science,monitoring_ai_review}), and this proportion grows as generated text re-enters the web and seeds subsequent generation.
The result is recursive generation chains whose outputs progressively diverge from human-written text.
Understanding the distributional properties of such recursive generation is a prerequisite for characterizing text provenance, yet the phenomenon itself (how distributional features evolve across generation depths) remains underexplored.

We study distributional drift in non-paraphrastic generation chains under controlled conditions, using eight base (pretrained) models from five families (Pythia, OLMo, Qwen, Llama, Mistral) spanning multiple scales.
We restrict to base models as a deliberate design choice: instruction-tuning introduces confounds (output length variability, format constraints, safety-driven distribution shaping) that obscure the generation mechanism's intrinsic behavior.
Preliminary experiments confirm this concern: instruct models show substantially degraded depth signal (\S\ref{sec:discussion}), motivating the controlled base-model setting as the appropriate starting point for isolating recursive drift phenomena.

Existing detectors \cite{fast_detectgpt,binoculars,ld_score,detectgpt}, like classical out-of-distribution methods \cite{ood_baseline,energy_ood,mahalanobis_ood}, provide binary real-vs-synthetic classification, conflating qualitatively different material.
A first-generation continuation retains much of the source distribution's lexical and structural properties; deeper recursive text exhibits measurably reduced vocabulary diversity and compressed perplexity.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text into generation depth classes (gen-0\,/\,gen-1\,/\,gen-2+) rather than producing a binary label, and refer to the overall framework as \emph{depth fingerprinting}.
No existing method addresses this task in non-paraphrastic continuation chains.
When repurposed as ordinal depth predictors, individual detection scores span a wide performance range (binary F1 from 0.53 to 0.68; \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}), making any single detector unreliable for depth discrimination.
Concurrent work on iterative paraphrasing chains \cite{broken_telephone,markovian_chains} analyzes convergence under semantic-preservation constraints; we study non-paraphrastic chains where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal.

We characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (including reference-model mean entropy, type-token ratio, and hapax ratio) drift monotonically with generation depth, while upper-tail features (entropy max, tail decay) remain near-stationary.
We hypothesize that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution with partial shape preservation; under this account, the softmax ceiling constrains upper-tail behavior regardless of input content, while variance shows moderate drift.
The combination of drifting and stationary features yields a 7-feature ensemble that achieves 3-class macro F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains).
However, the strength of this signal is prompt-type dependent: continuation chains exhibit stronger drift than elaboration or rewriting chains (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

We additionally report a negative finding: despite the effectiveness of quality-based data curation for pretraining \cite{fineweb,dolma}, depth-aware curation does not improve downstream language model quality compared to random subsampling at equal sample count (perplexity: 2.367 vs.\ 2.387).

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Task formulation.} We define ordinal generation depth estimation as a task beyond binary detection, providing a framework for characterizing how distributional properties evolve across recursive generation depths.
        \item \textbf{Empirical characterization.} We document differential depth response across eight base-model generators spanning five model families: a 7-feature ensemble combining drifting and stationary features achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.809 on cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation, with a single lightweight reference model, significantly outperforming individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
\end{enumerate}

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
\S\ref{sec:related} surveys related work on text detection, model collapse, and data quality.
\S\ref{sec:method} describes generation chain construction, feature extraction, and evaluation protocol.
\S\ref{sec:results} presents classification results, differential depth response analysis, and baseline comparisons.
\S\ref{sec:discussion} discusses mechanistic hypotheses and scope boundaries.

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\paragraph{Shape stationarity hypothesis.}
5	Upper-tail features remain near-stationary because the softmax architecture and sampling hyperparameters that determine distributional shape are fixed across depths; recursive generation shifts context toward high-probability regions (reducing entropy mean) without altering the generation mechanism itself.
6	This predicts stationarity until the model reaches its fixed-point distribution, a regime not observed at chain length $\leq$4.
7	Sampling ablation supports this: depth signal is robust at $t \in [0.5, 0.7]$ (${\leq}0.3$\,pp degradation) but breaks down at $t = 1.0$ ($-6$\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}), where sampling noise dominates distributional shape.
8	
9	\paragraph{Prompt-type dependence.}
10	Continuation chains yield the strongest signal (F1\,=\,0.781 vs.\ 0.730 for elaboration), with cross-type transfer at 0.753 (Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
11	Semantic-preservation constraints attenuate drift, consistent with \citet{broken_telephone}.
12	
13	\paragraph{Practical applicability.}
14	At the document level, gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 (37\% misclassification) is insufficient for automated filtering but suitable for flagging; at the corpus level, error scales as $O(1/\sqrt{n})$, making aggregate depth composition estimates reliable.
15	A detailed error analysis (Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}) confirms that errors concentrate in shallow gen-2+ samples where distributional drift is insufficient, consistent with DDR predictions.
16	
17	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
18	Model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse} describes degradation when models are \emph{retrained} on their own outputs; our inference-chain drift occurs without parameter updates, representing an early, reversible stage of the same narrowing.
19	Topic drift accounts for $<$9\% of feature variance ($R^2 = 0.082$), confirming it mediates rather than confounds depth signal.
20	
21	\paragraph{Scope boundaries.}
22	Three classes represent the practical granularity ceiling: 5-class LOGO F1 drops to $\approx$0.50, with gen-2/gen-3 inseparable (Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA fine-tuning recovers 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 (Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming signal beyond summary statistics.
23	Under text perturbation, the 7-feature ensemble achieves the highest unperturbed F1 with sublinear degradation; notably, LLM-simulated sentence regeneration (50\% edit distance) causes comparable degradation to 5\% random word replacement, confirming that depth signal captures generative structure rather than surface statistics (Appendix~\ref{app:human-edit}).
24	Instruction-tuned models show substantially weaker fingerprints (OLMo-Instruct LOGO F1\,=\,0.338 vs.\ 0.764 base), justifying our restriction to base models.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related}
3	
4	\subsection{AI-Generated Text Detection}
5	\label{sec:related-detection}
6	
7	Methods for distinguishing human-written from machine-generated text have evolved from statistical tests \cite{gltr,grover,release_strategies} to zero-shot reference-model approaches \cite{detectgpt,fast_detectgpt,binoculars,dna_gpt} and learned classifiers \cite{feat_aug_transformer,reliable_detection,ld_score}.
8	Recent work pursues diverse signals including intrinsic dimensionality \cite{intrinsic_dimension}, surprisal diversity \cite{diveye}, and distributional gap measures \cite{generator_barrier}; see \citet{wu_survey_2025} and \citet{jawahar_survey} for surveys.
9	A persistent limitation is that these methods produce binary (real vs.\ synthetic) decisions.
10	Recent multi-class extensions (role recognition in human-LLM collaboration \cite{beyond_binary}, multi-generator attribution \cite{semeval2024_task8}) discriminate among different \emph{sources} rather than recursive generation \emph{depth}.
11	Even when detection scores correlate with depth, they exhibit high cross-generator variance as ordinal predictors (binary F1 from 0.52 to 0.71; Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), because each captures a single distributional property that generalizes inconsistently \cite{paraphrase_evades,detection_possibilities}.
12	Our contribution is not a new detection method but the task formulation (ordinal depth estimation) and the finding that combining drifting and stationary features yields consistent cross-generator performance.
13	This is orthogonal to source attribution \cite{uchendu_attribution,munir_looking_glass}, which identifies \emph{which} model generated text; our LOGO evaluation decouples generator identity from depth.
14	
15	\subsection{Model Collapse and Iterative Generation}
16	\label{sec:related-collapse}
17	
18	Self-consuming generative models progressively lose distributional coverage \cite{self_consuming_mad}, and model collapse is inevitable without fresh human data \cite{curse_of_recursion}, though careful data mixing can mitigate this \cite{model_collapse_avoidable,strong_model_collapse}.
19	These studies focus on \emph{training-loop} degradation; our setting studies \emph{inference chains}, where a fixed model generates text conditioned on its own prior output without retraining.
20	
21	Two concurrent works are most directly relevant.
22	\citet{broken_telephone} analyze paraphrasing and translation chains, showing progressive information loss.
23	\citet{markovian_chains} demonstrate that semantic-preservation constraints induce attractor dynamics bounding distinguishable depth to approximately three classes.
24	We differ in studying \emph{non-paraphrastic continuation} chains, where the absence of semantic anchoring permits richer depth signal, and in focusing on \emph{estimating} depth rather than characterizing convergence.
25	
26	\subsection{Vocabulary Diversity and Stylometry}
27	\label{sec:related-diversity}
28	
29	Declining lexical diversity in LLM-generated text is documented in both training \cite{curious_decline} and deployment \cite{writing_diversity} settings.
30	Our surface features (TTR and hapax ratio) are classical stylometric measures \cite{stamatatos_survey,koppel_authorship} that we apply to inference chains, showing monotonic diversity decline across depths without model retraining.
31	We push beyond generator identity \cite{uchendu_attribution} to the \emph{depth} dimension, and show that diversity declines monotonically even under top-$p$ sampling \cite{nucleus_sampling}.
32	
33	\subsection{Data Quality and Provenance}
34	\label{sec:related-provenance}
35	
36	Scalable data curation relies on quality signals \cite{dsir,qurating,ccnet}; generation depth is a complementary provenance signal characterizing \emph{how many steps removed} text is from a human source.
37	Proactive watermarking \cite{watermark_llm,synthid_text,aaronson_watermark} embeds identifiable patterns, but watermark strength decays across multi-step chains \cite{chainwash}, motivating passive post-hoc methods like ours.
38	At the feature level, our NLL analysis connects to \citet{min_k_percent}, who use the probability tail for membership inference; we analyze the full NLL distribution for ordinal depth estimation.
39

1	\section{Method}
2	\label{sec:method}
3	
4	\subsection{Task Formulation}
5	\label{sec:task}
6	
7	Given a text $x$, the goal is to predict its \emph{generation depth} $d \in \{0, 1, 2{+}\}$, where $d{=}0$ denotes human-written text, $d{=}1$ denotes first-generation LLM output conditioned on human text, and $d{=}2{+}$ denotes text produced by recursively conditioning an LLM on its own prior output at least twice.
8	Formally, let $\mathcal{C}_0$ be a reference corpus of human-written text.
9	A generation chain of depth $k$ is defined recursively: $x^{(0)} \sim \mathcal{C}_0$, and $x^{(k)} = G(x^{(k-1)})$ for $k \geq 1$, where $G$ denotes stochastic LLM generation conditioned on its input.
10	We frame depth estimation as an ordinal classification task over three classes rather than binary real-vs-synthetic detection, enabling finer-grained provenance characterization.
11	Depths beyond 2 are merged into a single $2{+}$ class, consistent with monotonic feature convergence that compresses inter-class margins beyond depth 2 (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
12	
13	\subsection{Generation Chain Construction}
14	\label{sec:generation}
15	
16	We construct generation chains using eight generators spanning five model families: \textbf{Pythia} (2.8B, 1B) \cite{pythia}, \textbf{OLMo} (OLMo-2-1B) \cite{olmo}, \textbf{Qwen} (Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3-8B-Base) \cite{qwen3}, \textbf{Llama} (Llama-3.2-3B) \cite{llama3}, and \textbf{Mistral} (Mistral-7B-v0.3) \cite{mistral7b}.
17	This selection covers parameter scales from 0.6B to 8B and diverse pretraining corpora, enabling evaluation of cross-generator and cross-scale generalization.
18	
19	For each generator, we sample approximately 1{,}000 seed passages from English Wikipedia as $\mathcal{C}_0$.
20	The same pool of seed passages serves as gen-0 for all generators.
21	We use shared seeds across generators to ensure that cross-generator comparisons control for input content, isolating the effect of the generation model from source text variation.
22	In LOGO evaluation, gen-0 samples from the held-out generator's chains also appear (with the same text) in the training generators' chains, creating a potential train--test overlap for the gen-0 class.
23	We address this with a supplementary binary evaluation excluding gen-0 entirely (\S\ref{sec:results-baselines}).
24	Each seed is iteratively fed through the generator to produce a chain of depth 4 (i.e., gen-0 through gen-4), using the prompt ``\texttt{Continue the following text: \{text\}}''.
25	All generation uses temperature $\tau{=}0.7$, nucleus sampling with $p{=}0.9$, and maximum length of 256 new tokens.
26	The theoretical yield is $8 \times {\sim}1{,}000 \times 5 \approx 40{,}000$ texts; after removing generation failures, exact duplicates, and passages shorter than 50 tokens, 37{,}058 texts remain (Appendix~\ref{app:dataset-stats}).
27	For classification, depths 2--4 are collapsed into the $2{+}$ class.
28	
29	\subsection{Feature Extraction}
30	\label{sec:features}
31	
32	The seven features are motivated by two complementary views of distributional drift.
33	Reference-model features capture how the text's token-level surprise distribution shifts relative to a fixed model; surface features capture how lexical diversity contracts under recursive generation.
34	Together, they span both the generative mechanism (what the model produces) and the surface manifestation (how the vocabulary changes).
35	This two-pronged design is not post-hoc: it follows directly from the hypothesis that recursive generation induces a location shift in the NLL distribution (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}).
36	
37	We extract seven distributional features per text, organized into two groups based on what they measure rather than how they are computed.
38	
39	\paragraph{Reference-model features.}
40	A held-out reference model (Pythia-410M, chosen to be smaller than all generators) computes per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) for each text.
41	Although Pythia-410M shares the GPT-NeoX architecture with two of the eight generators, cross-family reference model experiments (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) confirm that depth features are not reference-specific (LOGO F1 varies by $\leq$0.013 across Pythia, OLMo, and Qwen references).
42	From the resulting NLL sequence, we extract five statistics:
43	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
44	    \item \textbf{entropy\_mean}\footnote{We use ``entropy'' as shorthand for token-level negative log-likelihood under the reference model, following convention in prior detection work. These are point-wise NLL values, not Shannon entropy of the full distribution.}: mean token-level NLL, capturing the average predictability of the text under the reference model;
45	    \item \textbf{entropy\_std}: standard deviation of token-level NLL, measuring the spread of per-token surprise;
46	    \item \textbf{entropy\_max}: maximum token-level NLL, capturing the most surprising token;
47	    \item \textbf{entropy\_min}: minimum token-level NLL, capturing the most predictable token. As generation depth increases, the floor of token-level surprise drops, reflecting the model's increasing confidence on its own outputs.
48	    Although entropy\_min shows near-zero marginal impact in leave-one-feature-out analysis ($\Delta$F1\,=\,+0.01\,pp), we retain it for completeness of the NLL summary statistics (mean, std, max, min) and because removing it does not improve performance;
49	    \item \textbf{tail\_decay}: proportion of tokens whose NLL exceeds the 90th percentile of the reference distribution (computed over $\mathcal{C}_0$), measuring how heavy-tailed the NLL distribution is relative to human text.
50	    Sensitivity analysis confirms stable classification (F1 variation ${<}$0.3\,pp) across thresholds from the 85th to 95th percentile.
51	\end{itemize}
52	
53	\paragraph{Surface features.}
54	Two features capture lexical diversity without requiring a reference model:
55	\begin{itemize}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
56	    \item \textbf{TTR}: type-token ratio (number of unique word types divided by total tokens);
57	    \item \textbf{hapax\_ratio}: proportion of words appearing exactly once (\emph{hapax legomena}).
58	\end{itemize}
59	
60	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
61	The grouping reflects an empirical pattern we term \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency and diversity features (entropy\_mean, TTR, hapax\_ratio) show strong monotonic drift with generation depth ($|\rho| = 0.60$--$0.63$); entropy\_min and entropy\_std show moderate drift ($|\rho| = 0.17$--$0.41$); and upper-tail features (entropy\_max, tail\_decay) remain near-stationary ($|\rho| < 0.07$).
62	This differential behavior, consistent with recursive generation compressing the lower tail of the NLL distribution while preserving upper-tail behavior, motivates combining both feature types.
63	As shown in \S\ref{sec:results}, the full 7-feature set significantly outperforms either group alone.
64	
65	\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
66	\label{sec:evaluation}
67	
68	\paragraph{Cross-validation.}
69	To evaluate generalization to unseen generators, we use \textbf{Leave-One-Generator-Out (LOGO)} cross-validation: in each fold, one of the eight generators is held out for testing and the remaining seven provide training data.
70	We additionally report \textbf{Leave-One-Family-Out (LOFO)} results, where an entire model family (e.g., all Qwen models) is held out, testing generalization across architectural lineages.
71	
72	\paragraph{Classifier.}
73	We use XGBoost \cite{xgboost} as the classifier throughout.
74	Gradient-boosted trees handle heterogeneous feature scales and nonlinear interactions without extensive hyperparameter tuning, and their feature importance scores support interpretability.
75	We use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}200$, $\max\_\text{depth}{=}6$, and learning rate $0.1$ for the 7-feature ensemble.
76	All other methods in Table~\ref{tab:baselines} (individual baselines and multi-detector ensembles) use $n\_\text{estimators}{=}100$ and $\max\_\text{depth}{=}3$ to avoid overfitting.
77	LOGO F1 is stable across random seeds (std\,$<$\,0.001 over 5 seeds), confirming that results are not sensitive to classifier initialization.
78	Alternative classifiers (random forest, logistic regression) yield comparable performance (Appendix~\ref{app:classifier}), confirming that discriminative power resides in the features, not the classifier.
79	We evaluated two ordinal-specific methods (CORAL \cite{coral_ordinal}, Frank-Hall ordinal ensemble \cite{frank_hall_ordinal}); neither significantly outperforms multiclass XGBoost (CIs overlapping; \S\ref{sec:results}), confirming that with only three ordinal levels, ordinal structure provides minimal additional benefit.
80	
81	\paragraph{Metrics and statistical testing.}
82	The primary metric is \textbf{macro-averaged F1} over the three depth classes, which weights minority classes (gen-1, gen-2+) equally against the typically easier gen-0 class.
83	We report per-class F1 scores and 95\% confidence intervals via \emph{percentile bootstrap} ($n{=}1{,}000$), resampling at the document level within each held-out fold.
84	For pairwise model comparisons (e.g., full features vs.\ ablated subsets), we use the \textbf{McNemar test} on disagreement tables.
85	For comparisons against detection baselines, we use \textbf{paired bootstrap} significance tests.
86	All reported $p$-values are two-sided.
87	We report four pairwise comparisons (ensemble vs.\ each individual baseline) in \S\ref{sec:results-baselines}; applying Bonferroni correction ($\alpha_{\text{adj}} = 0.05/4 = 0.0125$), all remain significant at $p < 0.001$.
88	Feature--depth correlations (\S\ref{sec:results-differential}) are computed on class-balanced subsamples (equal samples per depth class) to control for depth-class imbalance in the generation pipeline.
89	
90	\paragraph{Baselines.}
91	We compare the 7-feature ensemble against four single-score detection methods repurposed as ordinal depth predictors: Avg-LogProb, FastDetectGPT \cite{fast_detectgpt}, Binoculars \cite{binoculars}, and LD-Score \cite{ld_score}.
92	Each baseline score is used as a univariate feature in the same XGBoost framework under LOGO cross-validation, ensuring a controlled comparison.
93	
94	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
95	Since TTR and hapax\_ratio are mechanically length-dependent, we verify that depth signal is not an artifact of systematic length variation.
96	We conduct three complementary analyses: (1) length--depth correlation to verify absence of systematic length variation, (2) length--feature correlation to identify features with moderate length dependence, and (3) classification on length-matched subsets that equalize length distributions across depth classes (\S\ref{sec:results-classification}).

% Abstract — Depth Fingerprinting of Recursive LLM Generation Chains
\begin{abstract}
Recursive application of language models, where each generation step conditions on prior LLM output, produces text with progressively altered distributional properties.
We study this phenomenon under controlled conditions, restricting to base (pretrained) models to isolate the generation mechanism from instruction-tuning effects.
We formulate \emph{ordinal depth estimation}, classifying text by generation depth rather than a binary real-vs-synthetic label, and characterize a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency features drift monotonically with depth while upper-tail shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution with partial shape preservation.
A 7-feature ensemble exploiting this complementarity achieves macro-averaged F1\,=\,0.809 on heterogeneous cross-model chains and F1\,=\,0.762 under leave-one-generator-out evaluation across eight generators (binary F1\,=\,0.764 on cross-model chains), significantly outperforming all individual detection baselines ($p < 0.001$).
We additionally report that depth-aware data curation does not improve downstream language model quality over random subsampling at equal sample count.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
When LLM-generated text re-enters the web and seeds further generation, the resulting recursive chains exhibit progressively altered distributional properties.
We ask whether this drift is structured enough to estimate how many generation steps a text has undergone.
Studying eight base models from five families, we identify a \emph{differential depth response}: central-tendency features (mean entropy, lexical diversity) drift monotonically with generation depth, while upper-tail shape features remain near-stationary, consistent with a location shift in the token-level NLL distribution that preserves distributional shape.

However, this structured drift does not translate into training utility: depth-aware data curation offers no improvement over random subsampling at equal sample count.
\end{abstract}
